title: Making rivals depend on your system is the secret to America's three centuries of winning
dek: The Dutch, British, and Americans took turns as top dog not by blockading but by getting rivals to stake everything on their maritime system—once they can't live without the shipping lanes and markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective killer short of war.
why: Walter Mead breaks down America's three hundred years of success into a five-step strategy, extending it to China, the Taiwan Strait, and AI deterrence. He offers a durable framework for judgment, not news-driven opinions.
who: Overseas founders and those in the US-China supply chain, engineers studying the Taiwan Strait or drone warfare transformation, and investors focused on AI policy risk.

points.h: Unpredictability is a form of power
points.body: ‘Unpredictability’is not madness but a modern power strategy. Mead says post-Cold War US diplomacy relied on 'letting the world know where America's red lines are' as a pillar of stability, but Trump profits from the opposite: crossing lines, threatening allies, turning commitments into bargaining chips. He saw through a secret of the information age—the marginal cost of lying: the first lie is expensive, the thousandth is nearly free. Clinton, besieged by the Lewinsky scandal, discovered that shame lives only in others' minds; as long as you keep moving forward, the dogs bark but the caravan passes. Trump scaled that insight to industrial levels. The cost is borne by the US diplomatic system: when the world's top power itself becomes the unpredictable card, the alliances and rules built on predictability since World War II accelerate their unraveling.

points.h: The final step of global hegemony is cutting off
points.body: The Anglo-American maritime order won not through a single battle but a five-step playbook: first, open societies on islands—17th-century Holland tolerated heretics and Jews, and ideas and capital flowed in; then global trade, Dutch merchant ships traversing the world, wealth so abundant that paintings featured Turkish carpets and Brazilian parrots. Third, while continental powers fought over Silesia inland, you grabbed India and Canada globally. The fourth step is the riskiest: instead of imitating Spain's colonial blockades, invite the whole world to do business; the British navy fought pirates, benefiting all merchant ships; Germany and Japan were similarly invited in after the war. The final step is the trump card: once the other side cannot live without your grain, rubber, and shipping lanes, cut them off—Germany in World War I suddenly found Argentine grain and Malayan rubber cut off, and its economy collapsed.

points.h: All of China's efforts are to prevent the umbilical cord from being cut
points.body: Applying the same framework to China, one sees Beijing is acutely aware of its vulnerability. Mead says, suppose the mainland blockades Taiwan, and the US counter-blockades from a hundred miles off Taiwan's coast: oil can't come in, manufactured goods can't go out, soybean contracts with Brazil and Argentina become void—China's economy would be strangled. He has discussed these scenarios with officials and scholars at Chinese universities, and this concern always lingers. So China's energy policy must be read in parallel: on one hand, building oil reserves on a scale that surprises outsiders; on the other, aggressively expanding solar and hydro, while mining as much coal as possible. It's not schizophrenia but the same goal: pulling out, one by one, the weaknesses of 'dependence on the outside world.' He also warns America against retreating into isolationism—agriculture and AI both need overseas markets to sustain themselves.

points.h: Each technological dividend needs new institutions to match
points.body: Mead starts with the ownership society: at America's founding, the land was full of independent farmers; building a bridge might be good but it raises my taxes—that trade-off itself is political education. The railroad era paired with the Homestead Act, as the government gave land to railroad companies and farmers, growing a national market; in the 20th century, the suburban single-family home replaced the family farm, paired with tax-exempt municipal bonds and highways, becoming a new wealth distribution machine. Today that machine hits the housing wall: young people can't afford to live near work. His remedy is remote work and autonomous driving. The commuting radius expands from 40 miles to 75 miles, and usable housing land grows with the square of the radius—the physical space technology opens could support another two generations. But the prerequisite is institutional 'infrastructure'—he coined the term info-structure, meaning the institutional and regulatory rules that let AI actually land in hospitals and courts.

points.h: Silicon Valley tilts toward the Tech Hamiltonian camp
points.body: American foreign policy debate for centuries has been four schools: Hamiltonians want a strong state to pave the way for capital, Wilsonians want to spread liberal democracy, Jeffersonians fear big government, and Jacksonians are isolationist in peacetime but hit back hard when attacked. The post-Cold War establishment was a marriage of Hamiltonian and Wilsonian, but Trump brought Jefferson and Jackson into the mix. Mead says the truly notable new species is the Tech Hamiltonian. In the 1990s, tech companies liked to say 'we're global companies, Google has no borders, Washington can't touch us'; AI competition turned tech into a matter of national destiny. Economic stances changed too: old multinational car companies wanted borderless labor and markets, while Silicon Valley wants supply chain and IP security, even hoping employees are patriotic—selling code to China is shameful, and colleagues will report you. The commercial core shifting from old multinationals to tech nationalists is the underwater current of American political realignment.

points.h: The more equipment a great power has, the more it fears technological generational shifts
points.body: Mead has been to Ukraine twice. The first time at a drone factory, he saw them converting children's toy trucks into ground drones carrying mines to blow up tanks; months later, progress was unimaginably fast. The battlefield is now a gray kill zone, usually with only two or three soldiers operating together, and one of the hardest problems is 'how to evacuate the wounded'—you need a ground drone with a metal shield to drag people out, accompanied by a swarm of hunter drones to kill the enemy's attacking drones. He heard of one wounded soldier who took 63 days to be evacuated from the front line. Changes flip every six months. The irony for America: the great power with the most tanks and carriers is precisely the one most afraid of this parameter revolution—existing equipment turns from advantage to sunk cost. The Russian Black Sea Fleet has no major battles to fight, yet is trapped at home by Ukrainian small boats and drones.

points.h: The most important new variable in the Taiwan Strait is Japan
points.body: On whether the mainland will attack Taiwan, Mead's judgment: Beijing needs a very high probability of success to cross the threshold—failure would be catastrophic for the initiator. But between 'attack' and 'do nothing' lies a long gray ladder: for example, requiring all ships bound for Taiwan to first stop at mainland ports for customs clearance, or imposing a soft blockade—actions that change facts on the ground without triggering an armed US response. The truly new variable on the Taiwan chessboard is not America's attitude but Japan. The Japanese have publicly stated that if China takes Taiwan, Japan's independence is over; they are raising defense budgets, rewriting security doctrines, and reshaping national psychology. Historically, Japan has turned quickly when facing real threats. How steep Japan's learning curve is, and whether Beijing's calculations must factor in Japan, will be the key to the Taiwan issue in the coming years.

points.h: AI actually makes deterrence more credible
points.body: Applying Cold War deterrence logic to the algorithmic age, Mead points to a counterintuitive conclusion: deterrence succeeds only if the opponent is 100% convinced that 'if I do X, you will inevitably do Y, and you can and will do it.' As long as there is a human veto point in the decision chain—'I might soften at the last moment'—the commitment has a crack. Automating part of diplomatic decisions to AI turns retaliation into an executable, hesitation-free mechanism—making deterrence more credible. But this is the doomsday machine dilemma of science fiction: decisions of civilization-ending scale no longer require humans to bear the consequences. His own assessment of the issue is 'very interesting and somewhat puzzling,' and he doesn't think an answer has emerged yet.

terms.def: A new force in US foreign policy advocating state power to pave the way for tech companies, replacing old free-market multinational capital.
The institutional, legal, and regulatory frameworks needed for AI to safely land in settings like hospitals and courts, as distinct from physical infrastructure.
The American hawkish tradition of staying out of foreign affairs in peacetime but responding to attack with overwhelming force.
A method of strangling an adversary's trade without direct war, using customs, insurance, and port rules gradually.
